decomposition.reasoning: Standard Latin compound. Both trans- (across) and port- (carry) are productive in modern English. trans- appears in transform, transcend, transmit; port- appears in export, import, portable, porter. The decomposition is uncontroversial and helps learners see the common root across a family of words (transport, export, import, deport, report, support).

Classic Latin compound: ex- (out, from) + port- (carry) = carry out. The root port- is highly productive in English (transport, import, portable, portage, porter, sport, airport, seaport, deportation, etc.), and the prefix ex- is productive (exclude, extend, extract, etc.). Both morphemes are immediately recognizable to modern English speakers and learners can readily see them in other words. This is the kind of decomposition that unlocks learner insight.

Standard Latin compound. "Important" = im- (in/into) + port- (carry) + -ant (causing). The underlying sense is "carrying weight/significance into [a matter]", i.e., "mattering greatly". The port- root is highly productive in English (transport, export, import, portable, report, deport, support, airport) and -ant is a productive agent/causative suffix (brilliant, dominant, important, consultant, inhabitant). The im- prefix (in/into form before labial consonants) is productive (import, impale, implant, impose). All three morphemes are recognizable to modern English speakers and appear in many cognate words. This decomposition will help learners see the connection between "important", "transport", "portable", and other port- words.

Clear Latin decomposition. "port-" (carry) is highly productive in English (transport, import, export, report, porter, portfolio). The suffix "-able" (capable of being) is one of the most productive in English. A modern speaker immediately recognizes "portable" = "capable of being carried". This is the textbook example of a learnable morphological compound.

The word is a well-established Greek-Latin hybrid meaning "knowing beforehand" or "foreknowledge", specifically used in medicine to mean an advance assessment of disease course. The prefix pro- (Latin "before/forward") is highly productive in English (progress, propose, prologue). The root gno- (Greek "know") is also productive and appears in gnome, agnostic, diagnosis, and prognosticate. The morphemes remain semantically transparent and learner-recognizable. High confidence.

Greek dia- (through/across) + Greek root gn- (know, as in gnosis, prognosis, agnostic) + Latin suffix -ose (full of, as in verbose, grandiose, morose). The word originally meant "to know thoroughly" or "to distinguish by examining," which aligns perfectly with the morphological composition. Both dia- and gn- are productive in English (diagnosis, prognosis, cognition, recognize), making this a high-confidence decomposition.

Agnostic is a well-established English word formed from Greek a- (not/without) + gnost- (know) + -ic (adjective-forming). The decomposition is transparent and educationally valuable: the learner can connect "gnost-" to other English words like "agnosticism", "gnostic", and "diagnosis" (dia- + gnost- + -is). The Greek gnost- root meaning "know" is productive in English technical and philosophical vocabulary. High confidence.

Standard Greek compound: tele- (far, distant) + phon- (sound/voice) + -e (a common Greek noun-forming suffix). Both tele- and phon- are highly productive in modern English: tele- appears in television, telepathy, telescope, telegram; phon- appears in microphone, phonetics, symphony, telephone. A learner can readily see "telephone" as "distant sound" and recognize the morphemes in other words. No false-root trap, no opaque metaphor. High confidence.

Two productive Greek roots joined together: photo- (light) + graph- (write/record), literally "light-writing" or "recording by light". Both roots are highly productive in modern English (photo appears in photosynthesis, photon, photoelectric; graph appears in paragraph, biography, grammar, telegram). This is a classic transparent Greek compound that a learner can immediately understand and apply to recognizing related words.

Biology is a straightforward Greek compound: bio- (life, as in biography, biosphere, antibiotic) + log- (word/reason/study, as in psychology, geology, logic) + -y (nominalizing suffix forming abstract nouns). Both roots are highly productive in English, and the meaning "study of life" directly reflects the etymological composition. No false-root traps or opacity issues.

Two productive Greek roots combined with a standard Greek nominalising suffix. bio- appears in biology, biosphere, antibiotic; graph- appears in photograph, paragraph, graphite. The -y suffix converts the compound into a noun meaning "account of someone's life". No connective vowel needed as "bio" already ends in -o. High confidence: all three components are productive in modern English.

Standard Greek compound. "anti-" (against) is a productive prefix appearing in hundreds of English words (antifreeze, antisocial, antiwar, antitoxin). "bio-" (life) is highly productive (biology, biography, biosphere, microbe). "-tic" is a productive Greek suffix forming adjectives (democratic, sympathetic, problematic). The word literally means "against life" — referring to substances that kill or inhibit bacteria. All three morphemes are transparent and productive in modern English.

decomposition.meaning: study of, practice of, system of

decomposition.reasoning: Two productive Greek roots (geo- appears in geology, geopolitics; graph- appears in photograph, paragraph, biography) combined with the productive suffix -y (as in biology, psychology, history). The compound literally means "writing about the earth" or "description of the earth". Both roots are individually recognizable to modern English speakers, making this an ideal decomposition for vocabulary learning.

Straightforward Greek compound. Both geo- (earth, as in geography, geopolitics) and log- (study/word, as in biology, psychology, logic) are highly productive Greek roots in English. The -y suffix is a standard nominalizer forming nouns meaning "study of" or "science of". All three morphemes are transparent and appear in many other English words. No historical opacity; the modern meaning aligns perfectly with the morphological composition.

Two productive Greek roots: therm- (heat, as in thermal, thermostat) and meter- (measure, as in barometer, speedometer, geometry) joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-. The compound literally means "heat-measurer". Both roots are immediately recognizable to learners from other common English words.

Television is a transparent modern compound formed from the productive Greek prefix tele- (far/distant, as in telephone, telepath, telescope) + the productive Latin root vis- (see, as in vision, visible, evidence) + the productive Latin suffix -ion (result of an action, as in creation, nation, action). The word was coined in the early 20th century and all three components are readily recognizable to modern English speakers as meaningful units. High confidence.

Productive Greek compound. micro- is a well-known prefix appearing in microphone, microbe, microfilm, etc. The root scop- (meaning "look/examine") appears in telescope, periscope, stethoscope. Both morphemes are recognizable and productive in modern English, making this an ideal teaching example of how Greek morphemes combine to build scientific vocabulary.

Both "auto-" (self) and "graph-" (write) are highly productive Greek roots in modern English. Auto- appears in automobile, autonomous, autocrat; graph- appears in photograph, biography, paragraph. The compound "auto-graph" is transparent and etymologically sound—a signature written by oneself. This decomposition will help learners recognize these roots in other words.

Cardiology is a standard Greek compound meaning "study of the heart". The cardi- root (heart) is productive in English (cardiology, cardiac, cardiologist, cardiovascular). The log- root (study) is highly productive (-logy appears in biology, psychology, geology, etc.). The connective vowel -o- is standard in Greek compounds, and the nominalizing suffix -y is productive. This is a clear, learnable decomposition that helps a student recognize both the cardio- family of words (heart-related) and the -logy family (study of) in other contexts.

Two productive Greek roots (derm- meaning "skin" appears in epidermis, hypodermic; log- meaning "study" is ubiquitous in -ology words like biology, psychology) joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-, plus the nominalizing suffix -y. This is a standard Greek compound that a modern English speaker can easily recognize: the word means "study of skin", and all three morphemes (derm-, log-, -y) are productive in English.

Straightforward Greek compound: paed- (child, as in pedagogy) + iatr- (physician/heal, as in psychiatry, geriatrics) + -ic (adjectival suffix, as in democratic, economic). Both roots are productive in modern English medical terminology, and the -ic suffix is highly productive. The meaning "relating to the medical treatment of children" is transparent from the component parts. No etymological opacity or false-root traps.

Two productive Greek roots (dem- appears in epidemic, endemic; crat- appears in aristocrat, autocrat, bureaucrat) joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-. The -y suffix nominalizes the compound to form a noun meaning "rule by the people". This is a classic, well-known decomposition where all three morphemes are productive and recognizable in modern English.

Classic Greek compound from two productive roots: phil- (love, found in philanthropy, bibliophile, philanderer) and soph- (wisdom, found in sophomore, sophisticated). The -o- is the standard Greek connective vowel joining them, and -y is a standard Greek noun-forming suffix. The meaning "love of wisdom" is transparent and pedagogically valuable — a learner immediately sees how phil- + soph- = philosophy, and can recognize these roots in other words.

Two productive Greek roots joined directly without a connective vowel (phil- + anthrop- = philanthrop-). Phil- appears in philosophy, philophile, philodendron; anthropo- appears in anthropology, anthropomorphic, misanthrope. The -y suffix nominalizes the compound. High confidence: standard Greek formation, both roots are recognizable to modern English speakers, and the morpheme boundaries align with productive patterns.

The word decomposes into the productive Greek root "chron-" (time) and the productive Latin suffix "-ic" (relating to). The root "chron-" appears in many familiar English words: chronology, synchronize, anachronism. The "-ic" suffix is extremely productive (democratic, historic, economic). The meaning "chronic" = "relating to time" is transparent: a chronic illness is one that persists over time. No false-root traps or dead morphemes involved.

Classical Greek compound. "Chron-" (time) is a productive root appearing in chronometer, synchronize, anachronism, chronic. "Log-" (study of / word) is highly productive, appearing in biology, psychology, logic, etc. Both roots are connected by the standard Greek connective vowel "-o-". The "-y" suffix nominalizes the compound to mean "the study of time" or "the arrangement of events in time order". All morphemes are recognizable to modern English speakers and learners can find them in many related words.

Straightforward Greek compound. syn- (together/with) + chron- (time, as in chronology, chronic, anachronism) + -ize (make/cause to become, productive in English: modernize, capitalize, nationalize). The word means "cause to happen at the same time" — "make together-time". All three morphemes are productive and recognizable in modern English, making this an excellent vocabulary-learning decomposition.

Two productive Greek roots combined in a standard Greek compound. "Hydro-" (water) appears in hydrology, dehydrate, hydroelectric; "gen-" (birth/origin) appears in genesis, genetics, pathogen, hydrogen. The element hydrogen was named for its property of generating water when burned. Both morphemes are transparent and productive in modern English.

Standard Greek compound coined in the late 18th century (by Lavoisier) meaning "sharp-producer" or "acid-former", from oxy- (sharp/acid) + gen (produce/birth). Both roots are highly productive in modern English: oxy- appears in oxymoron, oxyacetylene; gen- appears in genesis, genetics, hydrogen, nitrogen, and countless scientific terms. The morphemes would be readily recognizable to a learner and the decomposition accurately reflects the historical coining of the term.

Genesis is a single Greek root morpheme meaning "origin" or "coming into being". It is a productive root in English, appearing in many derived words (generate, genetic, generator, oxygen, pathogen, hydrogen). The word itself is now fully naturalized into English and comes directly from Greek genesis (γένεσις), meaning "origin" or "creation". This is a clear, learnable single root that helps users understand its presence in compounds like "photogenesis" or "ontogenesis".

Straightforward Latin compound: dict- (say/tell, as in dictate, predict, verdict) + -ary (relating to / place for, as in library, January, secondary). The root is productive in modern English, and the -ary suffix is a common adjective/noun suffix. A learner can easily recognize dict- in other words and understand "dictionary" as "place relating to words/sayings".

Standard Latin compound: pre- (before) + dict- (say/tell) = "to say beforehand". Both morphemes are productive in English (pre- appears in prepare, predict, prefix; dict- appears in dictate, diction, verdict, dictionary). The meaning is transparent and synchronically decomposable. High confidence.

Standard Latin compound. The prefix contra- (against) is productive in modern English (contradict, contrary, contraception, contrast). The root dict- (say/tell) is highly productive and appears in many English words: dictate, predict, diction, verdict, edict. The compound literally means "say against", and the morpheme segmentation is transparent to modern speakers. Both parts are recognizable across many other words.

Verdict is a productive Latin compound: ver- (truth, as in verify, verity) + dict- (say/tell, as in dictate, diction, predict). The word literally means "something said truly" or "a spoken judgment." Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English, appearing in many other words a learner would recognize. This is a classic example of Latin root combination.

Manuscript is composed of two productive Latin roots: manu- (hand, appearing in manual, manufacture, manicure) and script- (write, appearing in prescribe, describe, transcript). The word literally means "written by hand" and the morpheme boundaries are clear and recognized by modern English speakers. Both roots are productive and appear in many related English words, making this an excellent vocabulary-learning decomposition.

Standard Latin compound: de- (a productive Latin prefix meaning "down" or "concerning") + scrib- (the productive Latin root appearing in prescribe, subscribe, inscribe, manuscript, describe) + -tion (the highly productive Latin suffix nominalizing verbs). All three morphemes are well-known and productive in modern English. The semantic composition is transparent: "description" literally means "the act of writing down/recording" and learners will recognize all three parts in other words (descend, define; scribble, script; nation, creation, action).

Standard Latin compound: in- (productive prefix meaning "in/into") + scrib- (productive root meaning "write", found in describe, prescribe, manuscript, subscribe) + -tion (productive suffix nominalizing verbs into nouns denoting acts/processes/results). The word literally means "the act of writing in/on something". All three morphemes are highly productive in English and recognizable to modern speakers.

Psychology is a standard Greek compound. Both psych- (mind/soul) and log- (study/word) are highly productive roots in English (psychology, psychiatry, psychosis; biology, geology, logic). The -o- connective vowel is the standard link between Greek roots. The -y suffix nominalizes the compound. This decomposition is uncontroversial and helps learners recognize these roots in related words like psychiatry, psychosis, biology, neurology, etc.

decomposition.meaning: relating to, of the nature of

decomposition.reasoning: Clear Latin decomposition. The root mem- (memory/mind) appears in other productive English words like "remember", "memory", "memorable", "commemorate". The suffix -ial is a standard Latin adjective-forming suffix appearing in "commercial", "residential", "testimonial", "material". Both morphemes are recognizable to modern English speakers and the meaning is transparent: "relating to memory".

Standard Latin decomposition. The root mem- is productive in English (memorial, memorable, remember, commemorate). The suffix -ory is a common Latin-derived suffix meaning "relating to" or "place for" (as in laboratory, dormitory, sensory). A modern learner can readily recognize both parts and connect them to other English words.

False-root trap. The word superficially looks decomposable as "un-" + "cle", but this is misleading. "Uncle" derives from Latin avunculus (mother's brother), which is itself a double diminutive formation from avus (grandfather). The "-cle" is not an English suffix; it is part of the Latin diminutive morphology now fully fossilized in English. A learner taught "un- + cle" would be misled into a false morphological pattern that does not reflect the word's actual etymology or structure. REFUSE.

False-root trap. "Island" looks like it could decompose as "is-" + "land", but this is a false analysis. The word comes from Old English "iegland" (ieg = island + land = land). In the 16th century, the "s" was inserted by folk etymology when the word was assimilated to "isle" (from Old French "isle"). The modern form "island" with its irregular "s" is the result of this historical confusion, not a productive prefix + root composition. Teaching a learner "is- + land" would be misleading.

False-root trap. "Butter" looks like it could decompose as "butt" + "-er" (agent suffix, "one who butts"), but this is etymologically false. The word comes from Greek "boutyron" via Latin "butyrum". The "-er" is part of the inherited Greek-Latin stem, not an English agent suffix. Decomposing it as "butt + -er" would teach the learner a false analogy and is therefore refused.

Two productive Greek roots joined by the standard connective vowel -o-, with the noun-forming suffix -y. Both crypt- (as in crypt, encrypted, cryptic) and graph- (as in photograph, paragraph, grammar) are highly productive in modern English. The meaning "secret writing" is transparently derivable from the parts. This is a classic Greek compound that a learner would recognize the roots in related words.

Two productive Greek morphemes. Xeno- appears in xenophobic, xenogeneic. Phob- is highly productive (phobia, claustrophobia, agoraphobia, etc.). The -ia suffix creates abstract nouns from Greek roots (as in phobia itself, dystonia, myopia). High confidence: learner can immediately recognize both roots in other words and understand the productive formation.

Omnivore is a standard Latin compound. The prefix omni- (all) is highly productive in English (omnivore, omnipotent, omnibus), and the root vor- (to devour/eat) appears in related words like voracious, carnivore, and herbivore. The final -e is a connective vowel/suffix common in Latinate noun formations. All three components are recognizable and productive in English morphology.

Clear Latin compound: herbi- (grass/herb) + -vore (eater of). Both morphemes are productive in English: herbi- appears in herbicide, herbarium; -vore appears in carnivore, omnivore, frugivore, insectivore. The meaning is transparent and the learner can immediately recognize these parts in many other animal-eating words. High confidence.

Standard Latin compound: carn- (flesh/meat) + -i- (connective vowel) + vor- (eat/devour) + -e (agent suffix forming a noun). Both "carn-" and "vor-" are productive in modern English: carn- appears in carnival, carnage; vor- appears in omnivore, herbivore, insectivore. The learner can immediately connect these roots to other words. High confidence.

Benevolent is a productive Latin compound: bene- (good, well) is a common prefix appearing in benefit, benefactor, benign; vol- (wish, will) is the root seen in volition, voluntary; -ent is the standard agent/quality suffix seen in different, apparent, patient. The meaning "good-willing" or "wishing well" is transparent and the morphemes are all productive in modern English. High confidence.

Standard Latin compound: mal- (bad) + vol- (wish/will) + -ent (agent/quality suffix). Both mal- and -ent are productive in English (malfunction, malice, current, patient, student). The root vol- appears in English words like "volition" and "voluntary", making the decomposition learnable and useful. The meaning "ill-willing" or "wishing harm" aligns transparently with the surface morphology.

Straightforward Latin compound. re- (again) + nov- (new) + -ate (causative suffix). The root nov- is productive in English (novel, innovation, novice), and all three morphemes are standard productive affixes in modern English. The meaning is transparent: "make new again".
